newsitem.title: MOLDOVA: Moldova expects $100 million World Bank loan.
newsitem.headline: Moldova expects $100 million World Bank loan.

text.p: The World Bank is prepared to grant a $100 million structural adjustment loan to Moldova if the former Soviet republic will speed up reforms, a senior Moldovan official said on Thursday.

"This week Moldova signed a Memorandum with the World Bank which opens the way for getting financial support for further reforms," Ion Ciubuc, Moldova's Prime Minister, told a news conference after returning from Washington.
Ciubuc said that the Memorandum stipulates five preliminary steps which have to be taken to unblock reforms.

The steps are boosting privatisation, agrarian reform, including land sales, strengthening the framework for public spending and reducing arrears, reforming the pension system and raising the pensionable age, privatising the energy sector.

The World Bank and the International Monetary Fund praised Moldova for an initial period of successful stabilisation, but said there had been serious cause for concern since the second half of 1996 due to the slower pace of structural reforms.
Moldova brought annual inflation down to 15.1 percent in 1996, keeping the currency stable and increasing external reserves to 315 million.
But structural reforms slowed, contributing to an eight percent GDP decline in 1996 and the build-up of payment arrears.
Moldova's foreign debt grew to over one billion US dollars, half of country's GDP. Production continued to fall and the foreign trade deficit widened in 1997.

Ciubuc said that the World Bank Board would meet in late June to discuss the Moldova loan. In the next two weeks the government must adopt the decisions stipulated by the Memorandum and present the respective legislation to the parliament.
Moldova expects to get the first, $35 million tranche of the credit, in early July.

"However, it will be hard to pass the legislation through parliament," said Ciubuc, hinting at the conservative majority, which passed few reformist laws after the December 1996 presidential elections and forming of the new government.

New president Petru Lucinschi and the Ciubuc government promised faster reforms, but they are not backed by leftist deputies, wary of approving unpopular measures ahead of parliamentary elections due in early 1998.
On Thursday, the Movement "For Democratic and Prosperous Moldova" called for the elections to be brought forward.

"We are loosing time... Only a new parliament would create a more productive government and take the country out of the crisis," said a declaration distributed by the Movement, set up on the basis of Lucinschi's election coalition.
It is headed by the deputy chairman of the parliament, Dumitru Diacov but is only backed by a minority of deputies.
